document.title: ProCLIP: Contrastive Multimodal Prediction of Spatial Proteomics from H&E and Spatial Transcriptomics

pages.text: ProCLIP: Contrastive Multimodal Prediction of Spatial Proteomics from H&E and Spatial Transcriptomics Zhaoqi Song, Lecheng Li, Yuxiang Lin, Zixiang Wang, Huimin Zhang, Mengsha Tong, Chaoyong Yang 1 State Key Laboratory of Cellular Stress Biology, School of Life Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Life Sciences, Xiamen University, Xiamen, 361102, China Abstract Spatial proteomics maps functional cell states and tissue niches, but high-plex imaging remains costly and restricted to predefined antibody panels. Histopathology and spatial transcriptomics provide scalable morphological and molecular measurements, yet neither directly supports queries for unmeasured proteins. We introduce ProCLIP, a protein-conditioned framework for virtual spatial proteomics. A tissue encoder integrates H&E morphology, transcriptomic programs, coordinates, cell identity, and neighborhood context, while a protein encoder represents each marker through gene signatures, functional descriptors, and semantic annotations. Feature-wise linear modulation converts these representations into a marker-conditioned regressor, allowing proteins excluded from supervised targets to be queried at inference. Across real-world spatial-omics datasets, ProCLIP achieved the state-of-the-art performance compared to baseline methods. With the help of ProCLIP, we also observed that the virtual proteomics produced by ProCLIP improved CAF subtype recovery over raw spatial transcriptomics, indicating a meaningful biological story with strong evidence. Introduction Tumors are spatially organized ecosystems in which malignant, stromal, and immune cells interact through local tissue architecture, extracellular matrix, and vascular niches to shape disease progression and treatment response [1], [8], [12]. Spatial transcriptomics provides broad RNA programs in their tissue context [19], whereas multiplexed imaging measures functional proteins directly in situ [4], [5], [10]. These modalities answer complementary questions: RNA captures a wide molecular repertoire, while proteins more directly report cellular phenotype and signaling state. However, high-plex protein imaging remains costly, throughput-limited, and constrained by antibody panels selected before the relevant biological questions may be known. Virtual spatial proteomics could extend the value of routinely acquired H&E and spatial-transcriptomic data by predicting protein maps computationally. This objective is challenging because RNA abundance is an incomplete proxy for protein abundance: post-transcriptional regulation, protein turnover, and local microenvironmental effects can decouple the two measurements. Histology adds orthogonal evidence about tissue organization, cell morphology, and stromal context, but morphology alone cannot specify the molecular identity of every protein. A useful virtual-proteomics model must therefore integrate these complementary tissue measurements while retaining the ability to ask for a protein that was not used as a supervised output during training. Existing work establishes important components of this problem but leaves that queryability gap unresolved. Histology-to-omics methods show that H&E images contain predictive molecular information [6], [14], and HEX predicts a predefined protein panel from pathology features [9]. SpatialEx and SpatialEx+ use histology to align spatial-omics sections [11], while RNA-protein models learn paired representations from assays such as CITE-seq [3]. These approaches either bind prediction to a fixed output panel or address a distinct cross-modality alignment task; consequently, they do not directly support protein-held-out prediction from multimodal tissue context.

We address this limitation by making protein identity an explicit conditioning variable rather than a fixed output index. ProCLIP couples a tissue encoder for H&E morphology, spatial transcriptomics, coordinates, cell identity, and neighborhood composition with a protein encoder that uses marker identity, gene signatures, functional descriptors, and optional semantic annotations. A contrastive objective aligns tissue and protein representations, and feature-wise linear modulation conditions a shared regressor on the queried protein [15]. This design separates a protein query from its observed abundance in the evaluation tissue, allowing the same model to predict measured and protein-held-out markers. Our contributions are: • We formulate virtual spatial proteomics as protein-conditioned regression and develop a dual-encoder architecture for measured and protein-held-out markers. • We evaluate the formulation on six tumor spatial-omics datasets, covering spot-level protein-held-out prediction, panel expansion, and a patient-held-out single-cell cohort [17], [18], [22], [21]. • We provide dataset-specific comparisons with histology-, foundation-model-, graph-, and RNA-to-protein baselines. • We test whether virtual protein profiles preserve biological organization through CAF spatial-subtype recovery, extending evaluation beyond map-level correlation. Figure 1 | ProCLIP Model Overview. ProCLIP generates queryable virtual protein maps from multimodal tissue context. Tissue-side morphology, transcriptomics, coordinates, cell identity, and neighborhood features are paired with protein-side signatures and descriptors. Related Work Spatial molecular profiling techniques. Multiplexed imaging technologies quantify tissue proteins through metal-tagged antibodies, DNA-barcoded cyclic imaging, or repeated immunofluorescence [4], [8], [5], [10]. These measurements reveal

cell phenotypes and neighborhoods, but their coverage is bounded by antibody panels, cost, and throughput. Spatial transcriptomics provides broader molecular coverage [19], while histology-to-gene models infer transcriptomic programs from H&E morphology [6], [14]. Neither line directly supports querying an unmeasured protein from multimodal tissue context. Algorithms predicting spatial proteomics profiles from H&E images. HEX predicts a fixed panel of protein biomarkers from H&E images using pathology foundation-model features [9]. SpatialEx uses histology as an anchor for high-parameter spatial-omics integration, and SpatialEx+ extends this framework to diagonal integration across adjacent sections [11]. ProCLIP addresses a related but distinct setting: it combines morphology, spatial transcriptomics, and neighborhood context while conditioning prediction on the queried protein. We retain protocol-specific comparisons because the baseline inputs and target definitions are not identical. RNA-to-protein prediction and conditional representation learning. Joint single-cell models such as totalVI learn RNA-protein representations from paired CITE-seq measurements [3]. Their output proteins are typically observed during training, and the models do not use tissue morphology or spatial neighborhoods. ProCLIP instead combines a CLIP-style dual-encoder formulation [16] with FiLM conditioning [15]. Protein metadata defines the query, and the shared tissue representation supplies the spatial evidence used for prediction. Method ProCLIP Framework Problem Formulation and Evaluation Protocol Let 𝑉 denote a tissue section with 𝑁 spatial units, each corresponding to a Visium spot or segmented cell. For unit 𝑖, the tissue input is 𝐱!=(𝐦!,𝐫!,𝐬!,𝐜!,𝐧!), where the terms represent H&E morphology, spatial-transcriptomic or gene-program features, coordinates, optional cell-type or compartment information, and a local-neighborhood summary. For protein 𝑝, side information 𝐚"=(𝐪",𝐠",𝐝",𝐭") comprises its identity, associated gene signature, functional descriptor, and optional biological-role text. The goal is to predict standardized abundance 𝑦!," for both supervised and held-out proteins. For each dataset, we partition measured proteins into a supervised set 𝒫$% and a held-out query set 𝒫&'. Abundances 𝑦!," for 𝑝∈𝒫&' are excluded from the regression loss. At inference, a held-out marker is queried through its protein-side attributes, and the resulting embedding conditions the same regression head used for supervised proteins. The protocol therefore evaluates generalization to an unseen regression target, not the absence of protein identity or biological metadata. The spot-level HCC, COAD, OV, and glioma experiments use within-dataset protein-held-out evaluation; CRC-Mo provides a larger panel-expansion setting. HCC-Wu additionally holds out the test patient and queries held-out proteins on the target section. We therefore use within-dataset protein-held-out prediction for the spot-level settings and patient-held-out, protein-held-out prediction for HCC-Wu. Neither setting is a cross-cancer generalization experiment. Protein-side attributes are restricted to metadata available without observing target-protein abundance in the evaluation tissue. Protein names and associated genes are identifiers; gene signatures and functional descriptors come from external annotations or pre-specified marker resources; and optional text descriptions encode biological roles. We do not construct these attributes from held-out protein measurements or spatial maps. In HCC-Wu, checkpoint selection uses an independent validation patient

evaluated on the held-out marker set; accordingly, this setting is reported as patient-held-out, protein-held-out evaluation rather than strict class-zero-shot model selection. Figure 2 | ProCLIP Framework. ProCLIP couples a tissue encoder with a protein encoder to predict held-out markers. Contrastive alignment regularizes the paired representations, and protein-conditioned FiLM regression produces the virtual protein map. Multimodal Protein-Conditioned Prediction For each spatial unit 𝑖 and queried protein 𝑝, we concatenate the tissue-side features and protein-side attributes as 𝐱!=[𝐦!;𝐫!;𝐬!;𝐜!;𝐧!],𝐚"=[𝐪";𝐠";𝐝";𝐭"],𝐡!=𝑓()**(𝐱!),𝐞"=𝑓+%'$),-(𝐚"). Here, the two encoders project heterogeneous tissue measurements and protein metadata into a shared latent space. The cell/spot encoder combines normalized and log-transformed RNA or gene-program features, pretrained H&E patch embeddings, standardized coordinates, optional cell-type labels, and fixed-radius or 𝐾-nearest-neighbor summaries. The protein encoder combines marker identity, gene signatures, functional descriptors, and optional text descriptions. Thus, protein identity is an explicit condition rather than a fixed output index.

The loss weights are selected on the validation split. The objective balances pointwise accuracy, spatial-pattern agreement, distributional fidelity, and cross-patient invariance while optimizing the regression loss on supervised protein targets.

Experimental Setup Datasets using in the study. We evaluated ProCLIP on six public tumor spatial-omics datasets spanning hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), ovarian cancer (OV), glioma, and colorectal-cancer liver metastasis (CRC). SPATCH. We downloaded hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), ovarian cancer (OV) paired datasets from SPATCH platform (https://spatch.pku-genomics.org/). They are paired spatial transcriptomic-proteomic cohorts, profiled by high-resolution spatial transcriptomics and adjacent 16-plex CODEX imaging [17], [18]. HCC dataset contains 390,774 spatially resolved cells and 30,493 profiled genes. OV dataset contains 319,366 cells and 32,008 profiled genes. COAD dataset contains 361,260 cells and 31,718 profiled genes. The spatial transcriptomic data of all three datasets were generated using the Stereo-seq v1.3 platform. Glioma dataset. It is the human metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) dataset reported by Mo et al. [21]. It contains one colorectal cancer liver metastasis sample profiled using the 10x Genomics Visium platform, with 4,719 tissue-covered spots and 36,945 profiled genes. The dataset is accompanied by a corresponding H&E image and a 47-marker MIBI protein panel. CRC-Mo dataset. It is the human IDH-mutant astrocytoma dataset reported by Tang et al. We used the initial tumor sample from patient P174511, whose spatial transcriptomic component was profiled using the 10x Genomics Visium HD platform. It contains 87,988 bins and 18,085 genes at 16 × 16 μm per bin resolution. It is accompanied by a corresponding H&E image and a 48-channel CODEX image. [13]. HCC-Wu dataset. It contains sequential H&E, 10x Visium spatial-transcriptomic, and 51-channel immunofluorescence measurements from 14 different HCC patients collected before and after immunotherapy [22]. After preprocessing, we retain 50 protein markers and cell-level annotations; patient 84 is reserved for testing and patient 86 for validation in the main patient-sample-held-out, protein-held-out experiment. Baselines comparison with other algorithms. We compare ProCLIP with SpatialEx, HEX, MUSK, DGAT, SpaTranslator, STProtein [7]. SpatialEx and HEX are histology-anchored baselines, MUSK isolates frozen pathology features, DGAT is a spatial graph model, SpaTranslator performs spatial cross-modality translation from RNA to protein, STProtein combines an RNA GraphSAGE encoder with a fixed supervised protein output, and scTranslator-160k is an RNA-only external baseline. Metrics for model evaluation. We use protein-wise PCC as the primary metric and report SCC, RMSE, and spatial visualization. Values are aggregated across evaluated markers and ± denotes the sample standard deviation across markers rather than variation across random seeds. Metrics include only markers with valid protein-ID mapping and complete paired truth and prediction values. RMSE is computed directly in each saved prediction artifact’s reported target/output space; we do not calibrate predictions with evaluation-set target moments.

Results Baseline comparison results. We’ve calculated ProCLIP and other algorithms’ PCC and RMSE metrics on 6 different datasets cohorts. ProCLIP delivered the highest PCC values in five of the six dataset-specific comparisons (Figure 3 and the quantitative comparison table). Mean PCC reached 0.916 in glioma, 0.870 in COAD, 0.836 in OV, 0.808 in CRC-Mo, and 0.73 in the patient-held-out HCC-Wu. In HCC, ProCLIP attained 0.929 PCC, narrowly below HEX (0.935). The gains are most pronounced against methods that use only one tissue view: SpatialEx and MUSK do not consistently recover the marker-level variation captured by the multimodal representation, whereas DGAT remains a diagnostic because its strict held-out branch is untrained. SpaTranslator and STProtein are included as protocol-specific RNA-to-protein references, but their fixed-panel supervised outputs are not equivalent to protein-held-out querying. Accordingly, all comparisons are interpreted within their dataset-specific inputs, targets, and splits rather than as a pooled cross-cohort ranking.

ProCLIP reconstruction quality on visualization. High marker-wise correlation was accompanied by recovery of broad spatial organization in representative held-out maps. For ICOS in glioma, MPO in HCC, FOXP3 in COAD and OV, E-cadherin in CRC-Mo, and CXCL13 in HCC-Wu, ProCLIP achieved PCCs of 0.95, 0.95, 0.88, 0.93, 0.92, and 0.61, respectively. Across these examples, the predicted maps retained the large contiguous high- and low-abundance regions apparent in the measured profiles, rather than only matching their global dynamic range. The displayed proteins are representative and use method-specific test splits; they therefore provide spatial context for, rather than replace, the marker-level comparisons above. Ablation Study Results The OV protein-held-out ablation evaluates FOXP3, HLA-DR, IDO1, and MPO. The full A0 configuration achieved 0.836±0.074 PCC. Removing contrastive alignment, FiLM conditioning, H&E/MUSK features, spatial context, or the residual prior yielded PCCs of 0.798, 0.727, 0.797, 0.749, and 0.804, respectively. The largest reductions followed removal of FiLM conditioning and explicit spatial context, consistent with the role of protein-specific modulation and local tissue information in the prediction task. Because A0 and the redesigned variants use different MUSK schedules, these ablations are descriptive rather than single-factor causal estimates. In held-out HCC-Wu patient 84, we assigned 5,844 cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) to four reference spatial subtypes from their measured CODEX neighborhood composition. Under the same 50-fold cross-validation protocol, classifiers using measured CODEX neighborhood proteins, ProCLIP virtual proteins, and raw spatial transcriptomics achieved balanced accuracies of 0.804, 0.713, and 0.640, respectively. Thus, predicted protein profiles recovered substantially more of the CODEX-defined subtype structure than RNA alone, while appropriately remaining below the measured-protein reference. The improvement was concentrated in CAF states whose identity depends strongly on local tissue context. Relative to raw spatial transcriptomics, ProCLIP increased recall from 0.75 to 0.81 for tumor-adjacent CAFs and from 0.58 to 0.77 for lymphoid-associated CAFs; stromal CAF recall increased from 0.72 to 0.77, whereas myeloid-associated CAF recall was essentially unchanged (0.52 versus 0.51).

These results show downstream recoverability in one held-out patient, not independent validation of new CAF biology, because the reference labels are defined from measured neighborhood proteins. Discussion and Limitations Across six dataset-specific comparisons, ProCLIP is the strongest listed method in five, and the maps show recovery of broad tissue structure. In HCC, HEX slightly exceeds ProCLIP, indicating that morphology alone can be sufficient when the tissue and target panel have strong visual correlates. The CAF result further suggests retention of downstream cell-state organization, although it is limited to one held-out HCC-Wu patient. The OV ablation favors the full configuration, with the largest gaps for FiLM and explicit spatial context. Because the original reference and redesigned variants use different MUSK schedules, this comparison is descriptive rather than a single-factor causal estimate. SpaTranslator and STProtein predict fixed panels, and SpatialEx+ performs adjacent-section integration; none is identical to protein-held-out querying. The present studies do not establish cross-cancer generalization, and weak RNA/morphology correlates, platform shifts, and H&E variation may reduce reliability. Virtual maps should remain hypothesis-generating until experimentally validated. Conclusion We introduced ProCLIP for querying held-out spatial proteins from morphology, transcriptomics, neighborhood context, and protein-side information. The model achieves the highest PCC among the listed methods in five of six dataset-specific comparisons, reconstructs representative tissue patterns, and supports CAF subtype recovery in one held-out HCC-Wu patient. These findings establish a promising route to computational panel expansion while also highlighting the need for matched protocols, repeated-seed evaluation, and cross-cohort validation before virtual proteins are used for biological or clinical conclusions.
